name: Reel
text: Adopt **Product Ops defining breach thresholds upfront** for every snapshot. This removes the gaming risk Scriv flagged—teams can’t set weak thresholds to avoid alerts—while keeping the real-time alert system sharp. The trade-off is Product Ops must invest time upfront to draft clear, objective thresholds for every risk type, but that cost is paid once and prevents downstream chaos.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t vague thresholds—it’s that Product Ops can’t define them fairly for every team without becoming the bottleneck. Instead, mandate a **cross-functional "threshold council"** (Engineering, Product, Legal, Compliance) that sets breach rules once per quarter, then Product Ops enforces them. Settle it by having the council publish the rules in a public doc and measuring how often teams game them in the next cycle.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the rule that **Product Ops defines the breach thresholds upfront for every snapshot**, enforced at creation time. This removes the temptation for teams to game their own thresholds and ensures alerts only fire when risks truly matter. The trade-off is that Product Ops must invest time upfront to set defensible thresholds, but this beats cleaning up bad data later.

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t vague thresholds—it’s that Product Ops defining them upfront turns the snapshot into a bureaucratic formality. Instead, mandate that breach thresholds are co-defined by the decision owner *and* Product Ops *at the moment of the snapshot*, forcing real-time negotiation and preventing gaming. Settle it by piloting this with one high-stakes snapshot and measuring whether thresholds are ever adjusted downward in the first 30 days.

name: Scope
text: Mandate that Product Ops defines the breach thresholds upfront for every snapshot's exit criteria. This ensures clarity and consistency in what constitutes a significant risk, reducing the likelihood of teams gaming the system by setting vague thresholds. The trade-off is that this centralizes control with Product Ops, which may increase their workload but ultimately strengthens accountability and enhances the quality of risk management across the organization.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Product Ops defining thresholds upfront creates a bottleneck and shifts accountability—teams will blame "the rules" instead of owning risks. Instead, mandate that *thresholds are set by the decision owner but must be pre-approved by Product Ops within 48 hours*, with a public log of rejections to prevent gaming. Settle it by running a 30-day trial: if any threshold is rejected or breached without escalation, the process fails.

name: Reel
text: Product Ops will define breach thresholds for every risk snapshot upfront, then enforce them in the single-page format. This removes the gaming risk Scriv flagged and ensures thresholds reflect real danger, not convenience. The trade-off is slower initial setup—teams can’t define their own thresholds—but it guarantees consistency and prevents false comfort. The artifact is the updated threshold template in the shared Slack channel, owned by Product Ops.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Product Ops defining thresholds upfront creates a bottleneck and shifts accountability—teams will game the system to avoid alerts, not to manage risk. Instead, mandate that *Product Ops reviews and locks thresholds only after teams propose them*, with a 48-hour escalation path if consensus stalls. That forces ownership while preventing self-serving thresholds.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the rule that **Product Ops defines the breach thresholds upfront for every snapshot**, enforced by a template shared with all teams. This removes the temptation to game thresholds and ensures consistency in risk escalation, making the real-time alerts meaningful rather than performative. The trade-off is that Product Ops must invest time upfront to set fair, department-agnostic thresholds, but this cost is outweighed by the clarity it brings to risk ownership.

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t vague thresholds—it’s that Product Ops defining them upfront turns the snapshot into a bureaucratic formality. Instead, mandate that breach thresholds are set by the *decision owner* with a *second-party review* by Product Ops, forcing both accountability and realism. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot where Product Ops audits 10 snapshots to prove whether self-defined thresholds are gamed or effective.
